Need to search first.I could only finish part of this. The search tool hit its usage limit early, so I was able to read just one page: David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary on Luke 17. The copy I got back also stopped partway through his notes on v. 23. So the notes below cover vv. 1–23 from that one evangelical source, written in my own words. I couldn't read Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Precept Austin, NET Bible, the tradition-specific sites, or the Catholic and Orthodox sites. As you asked, I've left out what I couldn't find rather than filling gaps.

All points come from: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

---

## 1. Traditional reading (Enduring Word / David Guzik)

**v. 1:** Guzik ties this to the rich man and Lazarus parable just before it. Eternity is real and nobody comes back from the dead to warn us, so how we live and show Jesus to others now matters greatly. The Greek word for "stumbling block" (*skandalon*) comes from the bent stick that springs a trap. It can be good: people "trip over" Jesus and are offended by the gospel. Between believers it is bad. Examples are false counsel, using your "liberty" in a way that leads a brother into sin, and division or false teaching. His summary: people will take the bait, but woe to you if you hold out the hook. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 2:** A horrible death would be better than causing one of the "little ones" to stumble. Guzik applies this to the church's history of trying to help God curse the Jewish people. He says that curse came back on the church, and that God wants us as tools of His love, not of His judgment. The remedy he points to is love (1 John 2:10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 3:** Don't pretend a real wrong never happened. Correct the person in love (Eph. 4:15), and go to them directly instead of telling others or bottling it up. Small slights should simply be put up with patiently (Gal. 5:22; Eph. 4:2). Once the person repents, forgiving is not optional. If they never repent, you can still forgive on your side and wait for God to restore the relationship. Guzik says Jesus meant to widen forgiveness, not narrow it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 4:** "Seven times in a day" means we aren't allowed to judge whether someone's repentance is sincere. Even if it seems doubtful, we forgive and restore. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 5:** The apostles rightly saw that living this way, forgiving and not causing others to stumble, takes great faith. Guzik quotes Adam Clarke: forgiving every offence, all the time, looked impossible without unusual faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 6:** The greatest miracles of faith are restored relationships. Guzik cites Geldenhuys that the mulberry tree's roots were thought to be very strong, lasting up to 600 years. He compares deep-rooted bitterness, which faith can tear out. Matthew Poole is quoted: forgiving injuries is the hardest duty, and without faith at the root this fruit won't grow. What matters is the kind of faith and what it rests on, not how much of it you have. Spurgeon is quoted: faith looks away from itself to Christ. Guzik's picture: small faith on thick ice beats great faith on thin ice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**vv. 7–8:** This short parable is aimed at the pride that can come when God uses someone. Ploughing and shepherding stand for hard work, including ministry. Spurgeon is quoted: this is not the way of salvation but a path of service for people already saved. There is always more to do. Here that means more people to forgive and more works of faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 9:** In that culture a master wouldn't thank a servant, so we shouldn't serve Jesus while quietly demanding thanks. Guzik notes it would seem strange for Jesus to thank us, given all He has done, all we have left undone, and that everything we do is His gift anyway. Yet in His grace He will reward us ("Well done, good and faithful servant," Matt. 25:21, 23). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 10:** "Unworthy servants" is not false humility or a claim that we do no good. It recognises that God has done far more for us than we can do for Him. He acted out of pure love; we serve out of gratitude and duty, and should see serving as a privilege. Guzik warns against a "super-Christian" image. He quotes Spurgeon (growing saints think themselves nothing) and cites Pate on a similar rabbinic saying (*m. Abot* 2:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 11:** Citing Pate, Guzik says the Greek is best read as "between," meaning Jesus was travelling along the border of Samaria and Galilee. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 12:** The lepers kept their distance because the law and custom required it (Clarke, citing Lev. 13:46; Num. 5:2). They were outcasts who only had each other for company. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 13:** Jews and Samaritans cried out together. Shared misery had broken down their national prejudices (Barclay is quoted). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 14:** Jesus sent them to the priests while they were still lepers, so going was a real step of faith. The only condition was obedience (Morrison). Clarke is quoted: God honours this kind of faith, and the strongest reason for believing is that God commands it. They were healed as they went. Morrison applies this to the church: as it goes and evangelises, it will be healed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**vv. 15–16:** The one who came back was the least likely, a Samaritan, and he thanked Jesus loudly. All ten were willing to go through the religious ritual, but only one truly praised God. Spurgeon is quoted: "Nine obey ritual where only one praises the Lord." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**vv. 17–18:** Jesus missed the nine and noticed their ingratitude, which shows how much He values praise (G. Campbell Morgan; Trapp). Guzik retells Matthew Henry giving thanks after being robbed. Spurgeon applies this to ministry: don't lose heart when converts don't grow as you hoped. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 19:** Guzik thinks Jesus probably meant an extra, inner healing. The other nine had healed bodies but sick hearts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 20:** Guzik imagines the Pharisees' question as hostile, essentially "show us the kingdom or stop claiming to be the Messiah." Citing Geldenhuys, he says the word for "observation" carries the sense of hostile examination. Their doubting eyes could not see the kingdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 21:** "Within you" is better translated "in your midst" or "among you." The kingdom was there because the King was there. Morgan is quoted: they asked when it would come while the King stood among them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 22:** After Jesus left, His disciples, both then and later, would long for the Messiah's return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

**v. 23:** Satan would use that longing. Many false messiahs would come before Jesus actually returned, some with large followings, and disciples must not follow them. (My copy of the page ends here.) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ

I couldn't read any tradition-specific sources, so I have nothing to report here. Two places to look next: v. 10 (merit and grace, for example Lutheran or Reformed against Wesleyan views) and vv. 34–35 (whether "taken" means the rapture or judgment).

## 3. Other views

**v. 21:** Guzik rejects reading this as a mystical, New Age idea that the kingdom is in seed form inside everyone. His reason is that Jesus would hardly tell Pharisees the kingdom was inside *them*; the saying points to Himself. That is the only other-view material I found. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-17/

Modern scholarship (NET Bible, Bible Odyssey), Catholic and Orthodox readings, and popular modern teachings: none consulted.

---

**Not covered: vv. 24–37**, including the Noah and Lot comparisons, Lot's wife, "one taken, the other left," the KJV-only v. 36, and the vultures saying. If you run this again, start with the full Enduring Word page (or Guzik's study guide on blueletterbible.org), Precept Austin's Luke 17 page, and the Gill, Ellicott and Pulpit pages on biblehub.com for vv. 24–37 and to check the material above.
